headline: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% in September as fuel costs surge, strengthening expectations of a Bank of England rate rise

terms.meaning: The Consumer Prices Index, the main official measure of how fast prices are rising.
Inflation leaving out volatile items such as energy and food.
The interest rate set by the Bank of England, which influences borrowing costs.

levels.headline: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% in September as fuel costs surge, strengthening expectations of a Bank of England rate rise
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.5% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 3.1% in August and above the 3.4% economists had forecast, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on 21 October.
Motor fuel prices were 29.8% higher than a year earlier. Energy costs have been pushed up by the conflict involving the United States and Iran and disruption to oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, which leaves Britain, a net energy importer, exposed.
Underlying pressures also increased. Core inflation, which excludes volatile items such as energy and food, rose to 2.8% from 2.6%, while services inflation stood at 3.7%. One economist said this could signal second-round effects, where higher energy costs feed into wider prices and wages.
The Bank Rate is 3.75% against a 2% inflation target. In September the Bank held rates in a 6-3 vote, with three members preferring a quarter-point rise to 4%. Markets now see a rise at the next meeting on 5 November as near certain. The next inflation figures are due on 18 November.
levels.why: A near-certain rate rise would raise borrowing costs for mortgage holders and businesses.

levels.headline: UK inflation climbs to 3.5% as petrol and diesel costs surge, adding to expectations of an interest rate rise
levels.body:
Inflation in the UK rose to 3.5% in the year to September, up from 3.1% in August and higher than the 3.4% that economists expected, according to the Office for National Statistics, which published the figures on 21 October.
Fuel was the main driver. Motor fuel cost 29.8% more than a year earlier. Energy prices have risen because of the conflict involving the United States and Iran and disruption to oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. As Britain imports much of its energy, it is particularly exposed.
There were signs of broader pressure too. Core inflation, which strips out energy and food, rose from 2.6% to 2.8%, and services inflation was 3.7%. An economist warned that this might show energy costs spreading into other prices.
The Bank of England's rate stands at 3.75%, with a 2% target. It held rates in September by six votes to three. Traders now expect a rise at the 5 November meeting, possibly the first since 2023. The next figures arrive on 18 November.
levels.why: A likely rate rise would make mortgages and loans costlier for many households.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5% as fuel prices jump, making an interest rate rise more likely
levels.body:
Prices in the UK rose by 3.5% in the year to September, faster than the 3.1% recorded for August and more than the 3.4% experts had predicted. The Office for National Statistics published the figures on 21 October.
The biggest factor was fuel, which cost 29.8% more than a year earlier. Higher energy costs are linked to the conflict involving the United States and Iran and problems moving oil through the Strait of Hormuz. Britain buys in a lot of its energy, so it feels these shocks strongly.
Core inflation, which leaves out items whose prices swing a lot, such as energy and food, went up from 2.6% to 2.8%. Services inflation was 3.7%. This hints that rising costs may be spreading.
The Bank of England's interest rate is 3.75% and its target for inflation is 2%. It kept the rate on hold in September, although three of nine members wanted a rise. Investors now expect an increase on 5 November. A final decision rests with the Bank.
levels.why: Higher inflation squeezes household budgets and could push up the cost of borrowing.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5%, driven by fuel, and interest rates are expected to go up
levels.body:
The cost of living in the UK rose by 3.5% in the year to September, up from 3.1% a month earlier, official figures showed on 21 October. Experts had expected 3.4%.
Petrol and diesel were the main reason, costing 29.8% more than a year ago. Energy prices have gone up because of the war involving the United States and Iran, and because ships are having trouble carrying oil through the Strait of Hormuz. Britain relies on imported energy, so it is hit hard.
Prices that leave out energy and food, known as core inflation, rose to 2.8% from 2.6%. Prices of services, such as haircuts and restaurant meals, were 3.7% higher. That suggests the pressure is spreading beyond fuel.
The Bank of England wants inflation at 2% and currently sets its main interest rate at 3.75%. Many investors expect it to raise the rate on 5 November, as three of its nine decision makers already wanted to do in September.
levels.why: Rising prices and possible rate rises both affect family finances.

levels.headline: UK prices rose by 3.5% in a year, and interest rates look set to go up
levels.body:
Prices in the UK are now 3.5% higher than they were a year ago, according to official figures released on 21 October. In August the figure was 3.1%. This rate of price rises is called inflation, and experts had expected a slightly lower number, 3.4%.
The main reason is fuel. Petrol and diesel cost nearly 30% more than a year ago. Oil has become more expensive because of fighting involving the United States and Iran, which makes it harder to ship oil through a key sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. Britain buys a lot of its energy from abroad, so it feels the rise.
Other prices are going up faster too. Services, such as restaurant meals, cost 3.7% more.
The Bank of England tries to keep inflation near 2%. It sets an interest rate, now 3.75%, that affects what people pay on loans. Many investors think it will raise that rate on 5 November.
levels.why: When prices rise faster, your money buys less, and loans can get more expensive.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5% mainly because of dearer fuel, and interest rates may go up
levels.body:
Prices in the UK were 3.5% higher in September than a year earlier, according to official figures published on 21 October. In August the rate was 3.1%. Economists had expected 3.4%. This rate of rising prices is called inflation.
The biggest cause was fuel. Petrol and diesel cost almost 30% more than a year ago, because the war involving Iran has made oil dearer and harder to ship. Britain buys much of its energy from abroad, so it feels these changes quickly.
The Bank of England aims to keep inflation at 2%. It sets an interest rate, now 3.75%, which affects what people pay on mortgages and loans. In September three of the nine members who vote wanted it to rise. Many investors now expect it to go up on 5 November.
levels.why: Higher prices and borrowing costs both affect household budgets.

levels.headline: Prices in the UK are rising faster, and the interest rate may go up
levels.body:
Prices went up by 3.5% over the last year in the UK. A month earlier the figure was 3.1%. This is called inflation. It means that things cost more than before, so your money buys a little less.
The biggest rise was for fuel. Petrol and diesel cost almost 30% more than a year ago. This is because there is fighting in the Middle East, which makes it hard to move oil around. The UK buys a lot of its energy from other countries, so it is hit hard.
The Bank of England is in charge of keeping price rises small. Its aim is 2%. It controls an interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. It is now 3.75%. Many experts think the Bank will raise it on 5 November. That could make mortgages and loans cost more.
levels.why: Higher prices and higher borrowing costs can make life harder for families.

levels.headline: Things cost more in the UK, and borrowing money may cost more too
levels.body:
New figures say prices in the UK are 3.5% higher than a year ago. Last month it was 3.1%. When prices keep going up like this, we call it inflation. It means a pound buys less than it did.
Petrol and diesel have gone up the most. They cost nearly a third more than last year. There is a war in the Middle East. It makes oil harder and dearer to move by ship. Britain buys a lot of its fuel from other countries, so we feel it.
The Bank of England wants prices to rise by only 2% a year. It can change an interest rate. That is the extra money people pay when they borrow. It is 3.75% now. Many experts think the Bank will make it higher on 5 November, to slow prices down.
levels.why: It affects how far your family's money goes each week.

levels.headline: Prices are going up faster, so grown-ups may pay more to borrow money
levels.body:
Prices in Britain are going up. Things cost 3.5% more than a year ago. That means something that cost one hundred pounds then costs about one hundred and three pounds fifty now. This is called inflation.
Fuel costs the most extra. Petrol and diesel are close to a third dearer. There is fighting in a faraway part of the world, and it makes oil hard to move. Britain buys oil from other countries, so we pay more.
There is a bank called the Bank of England. Its job is to stop prices rising too fast. It can change a number called the interest rate. When grown-ups borrow money, they pay back a little extra. The interest rate decides how much extra. Many experts think the Bank will raise it soon.
levels.why: Rising prices mean your family's money buys a bit less.

levels.headline: Why things cost a bit more now
levels.body:
Imagine your favourite sweets cost one pound last year. Now they cost a little more. When lots of things get dearer like this, grown-ups call it inflation. This month, prices in Britain are 3.5% higher than last year.
The biggest jump is for petrol and diesel, which cars and lorries need. There is a war far away, and it makes it hard to send oil across the sea. So the oil costs more, and so does the fuel.
There is a special bank for the whole country, called the Bank of England. It wants prices to stay steady, like a calm playground. It can change the price of borrowing money. If it makes borrowing cost more, people spend a bit less, and prices may calm down. Many grown-ups think it will do that soon.
levels.why: It shows why grown-ups sometimes talk about money being tight.

headline: Wall Street closes higher on 21 October as SpaceX results lift AI-linked shares; S&P 500 up 0.58% to 7,757.17

terms.meaning: An index tracking the share prices of 500 large US companies.
An index dominated by technology companies.
An index of 30 big US companies.

levels.headline: Wall Street closes higher on 21 October as SpaceX results lift AI-linked shares; S&P 500 up 0.58% to 7,757.17
levels.body:
US stocks closed higher on Wednesday 21 October, the last completed session. The S&P 500 rose about 0.58% to 7,757.17, its third straight daily gain. The Nasdaq Composite gained about 1.05% to roughly 26,702.86, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 360.21 points, or 0.69%, to 52,856.09.
The main driver was quarterly results from SpaceX, which were described as blowout and fuelled investor enthusiasm for the artificial intelligence trade. Shares of chipmakers Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices rose, and Nvidia was also lifted. A raised revenue outlook from Super Micro Computer added to the mood.
The move came as investors weigh elevated inflation and the prospect of further interest rate rises. The Federal Reserve meets on 28 October, with the benchmark rate currently at 3.75% to 4%. Another session follows on Thursday.
The figures are CNBC's closing numbers; other data providers show slightly different levels from different timestamps.
levels.why: Share prices feed into pensions, savings and investor confidence about the economy.

levels.headline: US stocks end higher on 21 October as SpaceX results boost AI-related shares
levels.body:
Wall Street ended Wednesday 21 October higher, the latest completed trading day. The S&P 500 closed up about 0.58% at 7,757.17, a third straight daily rise. The Nasdaq Composite gained roughly 1.05% to about 26,702.86. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 360.21 points, or 0.69%, to finish at 52,856.09.
The lift came largely from quarterly results from SpaceX, which excited investors about artificial intelligence. Shares in chipmakers such as Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices rose, and Nvidia gained. Super Micro Computer also helped after raising its expected revenue.
Markets remain watchful about inflation and interest rates. The Federal Reserve's next decision is on 28 October. Its main rate is in a range of 3.75% to 4%, after a rise in September, and traders are debating whether it will raise again.
These are CNBC's closing figures. Other sources give slightly different numbers.
levels.why: Moves in US shares influence markets worldwide, including pension funds.

levels.headline: S&P 500 rises 0.58% as SpaceX results lift tech and chip shares
levels.body:
US share prices closed higher on Wednesday 21 October, the most recent full trading day. The S&P 500, which tracks 500 large American companies, rose about 0.58% to 7,757.17. This was its third gain in a row. The Nasdaq, which has many technology firms, rose about 1.05% to roughly 26,702.86. The Dow Jones index gained 360.21 points, or 0.69%, to 52,856.09.
Investors were excited by strong results from SpaceX. This lifted companies linked to artificial intelligence. Chipmakers Micron and AMD rose, and Nvidia gained too. Super Micro Computer raised its sales forecast, which also helped.
Still, investors are nervous about inflation. The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, meets on 28 October. Its rate is between 3.75% and 4%, and some traders think it could rise again.
levels.why: Stock markets shape savings and show how confident investors feel.

levels.headline: US shares rise for a third day after strong results from SpaceX
levels.body:
US shares rose again on Wednesday 21 October. The S&P 500 index, which tracks 500 large American companies, gained about 0.58% to close at 7,757.17. That was its third rise in a row. The Nasdaq rose about 1.05% and the Dow about 0.69%, to 52,856.09.
The reason was a strong set of results from SpaceX. This made investors more excited about artificial intelligence, or AI, which many expect to make firms richer. Companies that make computer chips, including Micron, AMD and Nvidia, saw their shares go up.
The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, makes its next interest rate decision on 28 October. Its rate is now between 3.75% and 4%, and investors are watching in case it goes up again.
levels.why: Share prices show how confident investors are about companies and the economy.

levels.headline: US shares rise as strong SpaceX results boost technology companies
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States went up on Wednesday 21 October, the latest day when markets were fully open. The S&P 500, a measure of 500 big companies, gained about 0.58% and closed at 7,757.17. That was the third day in a row it had risen. The Nasdaq, full of technology firms, rose about 1.05% to roughly 26,702.86. The Dow, which follows 30 large companies, went up 0.69% to 52,856.09.
The boost came from very strong results from SpaceX. Investors hope that artificial intelligence will make companies richer, so shares in firms making computer chips also went up.
Still, there is some worry about prices rising too fast. The US central bank, called the Federal Reserve, meets on 28 October to decide on interest rates. They are now between 3.75% and 4%.
levels.why: Many pensions and savings are invested in shares.

levels.headline: American shares rose on Wednesday after good news from SpaceX
levels.body:
On Wednesday 21 October, share prices in the United States went up. A share is a small piece of a company. People buy shares hoping the company does well. The main index, the S&P 500, rose by about 0.58% to 7,757.17. An index is a number that shows how a group of shares is doing. This was the third day in a row of rises. The Nasdaq index rose by about 1.05% and the Dow rose by about 0.69%.
The reason was good results from SpaceX. People think artificial intelligence, or AI, will be important. So firms that make computer chips, such as Micron and AMD, also did well.
The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, meets on 28 October to decide on interest rates, which affect the cost of borrowing.
levels.why: Share prices show how hopeful people are about companies and the economy.

levels.headline: US share prices went up after a big company said it did very well
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States went up on Wednesday. A share is a tiny slice of a company that you can buy. If the company does well, the slice can be worth more. A big number called the S&P 500 tracks 500 large companies. It went up by about half of one percent, to 7,757.17. It had also gone up on the two days before.
Two other numbers also rose. The Nasdaq, which follows lots of tech firms, went up by about 1%. The Dow, which follows 30 big firms, went up by about 0.7%.
The news came from a company called SpaceX, which said its results were very good. Companies that make computer chips for artificial intelligence, or AI, also saw their shares rise.
levels.why: It helps show whether people feel hopeful about businesses.

levels.headline: American shares go up again, helped by good news about technology
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States went up for the third day running on Wednesday. A share is a small piece of a company, and its price changes with how well people think the firm is doing. The main measure, the S&P 500, went up by about 0.58%, to 7,757.17. Two other measures, the Nasdaq and the Dow, also went up.
The news that helped most came from SpaceX, which reported very strong results. People hope that artificial intelligence, or AI, will help companies earn more, so firms that make the chips for AI computers did well too.
The US central bank will decide on 28 October whether to change its interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money.
levels.why: Many families have savings or pensions linked to share prices.

levels.headline: American company shares went up on Wednesday
levels.body:
Shares are small pieces of companies. People buy them and hope they will be worth more later. On Wednesday, many shares in America went up in price. A number called the S&P 500 shows how 500 big companies are doing. It rose by a little over half of one percent, to 7,757.17. It was the third day in a row that it went up.
Other numbers went up too. One called the Nasdaq follows lots of computer companies. It rose by about one percent. One called the Dow follows thirty big companies. It rose by about seven tenths of one percent.
The reason was good news from a company called SpaceX. It said it had done very well. That made people hopeful about companies that make computer chips and artificial intelligence, called AI.
levels.why: Share prices show how hopeful people feel about companies.

levels.headline: A good day for company shares in America
levels.body:
Think of a company as a big cake. A share is one slice. If people think the cake is tasty, they will pay more for a slice. On Wednesday, lots of company slices in America cost a bit more.
There is a big scoreboard called the S&P 500. It adds up how 500 big companies are doing. It went up by about half of one percent. That is the third day in a row it went up. Two other scoreboards, called the Nasdaq and the Dow, went up too.
The good news came from a company called SpaceX. It told everyone it had done really well. People got excited about computer chips and smart machines, called AI. Those companies went up as well. Grown-ups watch these scoreboards to see how hopeful people feel.
levels.why: It is a bit like watching a scoreboard to see who is winning.

headline: Burnham and Healey face first Budget on 28 October with tax rises not ruled out and borrowing costs under scrutiny

terms.meaning: The government's yearly statement of tax and spending plans.
Bonds the UK government sells to borrow money.
A one-off tax on unusually high profits.

levels.headline: Burnham and Healey face first Budget on 28 October with tax rises not ruled out and borrowing costs under scrutiny
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will deliver the first Budget of Andy Burnham's government on Wednesday 28 October. Burnham became Prime Minister on 20 July 2026, succeeding Keir Starmer, and appointed Healey, previously defence secretary, as Chancellor.
Burnham has refused to rule out tax rises, and British press reports suggest a windfall tax on banks may be considered. Healey has spoken of building a fiscal buffer against uncertainty. Defence funding is a key issue, with Burnham saying the defence investment plan must be worked through before the Budget.
Markets are watching closely. One commentary says Britain has the highest government borrowing costs in the G7, and a former Bank of England chief economist has warned the country is on thin ice and must act to reassure financial markets, while avoiding painful tax rises.
These details come from reporting over recent weeks and may change before the Budget.
levels.why: The Budget sets taxes and spending that affect households, businesses and public services.

levels.headline: Healey's first Budget due on 28 October, with tax rises possible and markets on alert
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will present the first Budget of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government on 28 October. Burnham took over from Keir Starmer on 20 July 2026 and chose Healey, formerly the defence secretary, to run the Treasury.
The Prime Minister has not ruled out raising taxes. Newspapers report that a windfall tax on banks could be on the table. Healey has talked about holding a buffer against uncertainty. Defence spending is a major question, and Burnham has said the plan to fund it needs to be settled before the Budget.
Investors are watching. One commentary says UK government borrowing costs are the highest in the G7. A former Bank of England chief economist said the country is on thin ice and must reassure markets, ideally without painful tax rises.
The details come from recent reports and may shift before the day.
levels.why: What the Chancellor announces will affect tax bills and public spending.

levels.headline: Budget on 28 October: new Chancellor Healey under pressure on tax and borrowing
levels.body:
The new Chancellor, John Healey, will announce the government's Budget on Wednesday 28 October. It is the first Budget under Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who replaced Keir Starmer in July. Healey was previously the defence secretary.
Burnham has not ruled out higher taxes, and some newspapers say banks could face a windfall tax, which is a one-off charge on very high profits. Healey has spoken about keeping a safety buffer in the public finances. Paying for defence is also a big question.
Financial markets are paying attention. One commentary says the UK pays the highest rates in the G7 to borrow money. A former Bank of England chief economist said the government should show that it can control its finances, and he argued against painful tax rises.
These reports may change before the Budget itself.
levels.why: The Budget decides how much tax people and firms pay and how money is spent.

levels.headline: Britain's new Chancellor prepares his first Budget, with tax rises possible
levels.body:
John Healey will give the UK's Budget on Wednesday 28 October. This is when the Chancellor, who looks after the country's money, explains plans for taxes and spending. It is the first Budget since Andy Burnham became Prime Minister in July, taking over from Keir Starmer. Healey used to be the defence secretary.
Burnham has said he will not rule out putting taxes up. Some newspapers say banks could be asked to pay a windfall tax, a one-off charge on extra big profits. Healey wants to keep a cushion in case something goes wrong. How to pay for defence is another big question.
Investors are watching too. Some say the government pays more than any other G7 country to borrow money. A former Bank of England economist said ministers must reassure markets.
levels.why: It could change what you or your family pay in tax.

levels.headline: A big money announcement is coming in the UK on 28 October
levels.body:
On Wednesday 28 October, the person in charge of the UK's money will make a big announcement. His name is John Healey and his job is called Chancellor. The announcement is called the Budget. It says how much tax people will pay and how the government will spend money on things like hospitals, schools and defence.
Andy Burnham became Prime Minister in July, and this is the first Budget since then. Burnham has not said taxes will stay the same. Newspapers say banks might have to pay an extra one-off tax because they have made large profits.
The government also borrows money, and some experts say it is paying a high price for that. People are watching to see whether the Chancellor can reassure them.
levels.why: The Budget affects the money that families and schools have.

levels.headline: A big UK money announcement is due on 28 October
levels.body:
On Wednesday 28 October, the Chancellor, John Healey, will give the UK's Budget. This is a yearly plan that says how much tax people and businesses will pay and how much the government will spend. It is the first Budget since Andy Burnham became Prime Minister in July.
Burnham has not ruled out putting taxes up. Newspapers say banks could be asked to pay a one-off windfall tax on very large profits. Paying for defence is a big question too.
The government also borrows money by selling bonds called gilts. One commentary says UK borrowing costs are the highest in the G7, so investors will be watching closely to see whether the plan looks careful.
levels.why: The Budget touches taxes, public services and the cost of government borrowing.

levels.headline: The UK's Budget is coming soon, and it could change taxes
levels.body:
A Budget is a plan for how a country gets and spends its money. In the UK, the Chancellor shares it once a year. This year it is on Wednesday 28 October. The Chancellor is John Healey. He works for the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, who took over in July.
Getting money means collecting taxes from people and companies. Spending means paying for things like hospitals, schools, the army and roads. The government has not promised that taxes will stay the same. Newspapers say banks might be asked to pay an extra tax.
The government also borrows money. Some experts say it costs a lot to borrow right now. They want the government to show that it has a careful plan.
levels.why: Taxes and spending touch most people's daily lives.

levels.headline: The government will say how it plans to use the country's money
levels.body:
Every year, the people who run the UK share a plan for money. It is called the Budget. This year it is on 28 October. A man called John Healey will tell everyone the plan. His job is Chancellor. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, is his boss.
The plan says how much tax people will pay. Tax is money that people and companies give to the government. The government uses it to pay for schools, hospitals and the army. It might need more money this year. It has not promised that taxes will stay the same.
The government also borrows money, a bit like a loan. Some experts say it costs a lot at the moment, so they want a careful plan.
levels.why: It decides how money is shared for things we all use.

levels.headline: The country gets a money plan soon
levels.body:
Imagine your whole school had one big pot of money. The pot pays for books, teachers and a clean building. The pot is filled by everyone giving a little. In a country, that pot is paid for by taxes. Once a year, the person in charge of it explains the plan. That plan is called the Budget.
This year the plan will be told on 28 October by a man called John Healey. He is the Chancellor. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, is the leader of the country.
Grown-ups think the pot might need more money. The government has not promised it will not ask for more tax. Some grown-ups also worry that borrowing money is costly right now. So they will listen carefully.
levels.why: The plan decides what the country can pay for.

levels.headline: A plan for the country's money
levels.body:
Think about pocket money. You get a little each week. You decide how much to spend and how much to save. A country has to do something like that too, but with much more money.
Once a year, the person in charge of the country's money tells everyone the plan. He is called the Chancellor. This year his name is John Healey. The plan is called the Budget. He will share it on 28 October.
The money comes from taxes, which are small amounts that grown-ups and companies pay. It is spent on things like schools, hospitals and the army. Grown-ups think the plan might ask some people to pay a bit more. Everyone will be listening to find out.
levels.why: The country's pocket money pays for the things we all share.

headline: UK says RAF Fairford incident was almost certainly directed by Iran's IRGC, as police investigation continues

terms.meaning: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a powerful branch of its armed forces.
Officially naming who is responsible for an attack or plot.
Penalties, such as asset freezes, imposed on people or countries.

levels.headline: UK says RAF Fairford incident was almost certainly directed by Iran's IRGC, as police investigation continues
levels.body:
On 12 October the Home Secretary told Parliament that the incident near RAF Fairford was highly likely to have been coordinated by a known individual based in Iran and almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Prime Minister Andy Burnham made the same assessment to the Commons.
On 27 September five men were arrested near the Gloucestershire base on suspicion of explosives offences, later re-arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. Two more men were arrested in London, one a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national. All seven remain on police bail. Reports differ on the evidence, with one early account citing explosives and a later report saying petrol but no explosives were found.
The Foreign Secretary summoned Iran's ambassador, and the government sanctioned two individuals. Many countries backed the attribution. Iran's embassy rejects any involvement. Donald Trump said the US moved B-1 bombers from the base.
levels.why: It deepens tension between the UK and Iran and affects security policy.

levels.headline: UK blames Iran's IRGC for the RAF Fairford security incident, which Tehran denies
levels.body:
The Home Secretary said on 12 October that the incident near RAF Fairford was highly likely to have been coordinated by a known individual in Iran and almost certainly directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs the same.
Five men were arrested near the Gloucestershire air base on 27 September on suspicion of explosives offences, and then on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. Two more men were arrested in London, including a 25-year-old with UK and Iranian nationality. All seven are on police bail. Early reports mentioned explosives, but a later report said police found petrol and no explosives.
The government summoned Iran's ambassador and sanctioned two individuals. Several countries supported the UK's conclusion. Iran's embassy in London said it rejects the claim. President Trump said US B-1 bombers were moved from the base.
levels.why: It affects national security and Britain's relations with Iran and the US.

levels.headline: The UK says Iran's Revolutionary Guard was behind the RAF Fairford scare
levels.body:
The Home Secretary told Parliament on 12 October that the security incident at RAF Fairford was very likely organised by a known person in Iran and almost certainly directed by Iran's Revolutionary Guard, known as the IRGC. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said the same.
On 27 September police arrested five men near the base in Gloucestershire. They were first held on suspicion of explosives offences, then of preparing a terrorist act. Two more men were arrested in London, one a 25-year-old with both UK and Iranian nationality. All seven are on police bail. Early reports spoke of explosives, but a later one said only petrol was found.
The government called in Iran's ambassador and put sanctions on two people. Other countries backed the UK. Iran denies any part. President Trump said the US had moved bombers away.
levels.why: It raises questions about the safety of military sites and UK-Iran relations.

levels.headline: UK says Iran's Revolutionary Guard was almost certainly behind a scare at RAF Fairford
levels.body:
The government has said that a security scare at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire was highly likely to have been organised by someone in Iran and almost certainly directed by the Revolutionary Guard, a powerful branch of Iran's armed forces. The Home Secretary and the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, told Parliament this on 12 October.
Police arrested five men near the base on 27 September and two more in London. All seven are on bail while the investigation continues. No one has been found guilty. Reports differ on what police found, with one early account mentioning explosives and a later one saying petrol.
Iran's ambassador was called in, and two people have been sanctioned. Iran says it had no part in it.
levels.why: It affects national security and the UK's relations with Iran.

levels.headline: UK blames Iran for a security scare at an RAF base
levels.body:
The Home Secretary told MPs on 12 October that a security scare at RAF Fairford, an air base in Gloucestershire, was very likely planned by someone in Iran. She said it was almost certainly directed by Iran's Revolutionary Guard, a powerful part of its armed forces. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, agreed.
On 27 September police arrested five men near the base. They were held on suspicion of explosives offences, and later of preparing an act of terrorism. Two more men were arrested in London. All seven have been released on bail while police keep investigating. Reports differ on what was found. One said explosives, a later one said petrol.
The UK has called in Iran's ambassador and put sanctions on two people. Iran says it had nothing to do with it.
levels.why: It could change how safe the UK feels and how it deals with Iran.

levels.headline: The UK says Iran was behind a scare at an air base
levels.body:
The government has said that a security scare at an air force base was very likely organised by Iran. The base is called RAF Fairford, in Gloucestershire. On 12 October, the Home Secretary told MPs that it was almost certainly directed by a powerful Iranian group called the Revolutionary Guard.
On 27 September the police arrested five men near the base. Then they arrested two more men in London. All seven are out on bail while police look into what happened. The police say they are still working it out. Some reports said there were explosives. A later one said there was only petrol.
The UK has asked Iran's ambassador to come in and explain. It has also punished two people with sanctions. Iran says it was not involved.
levels.why: It is about keeping people safe and how countries get on.

levels.headline: The UK says Iran was behind a danger at an air base
levels.body:
The UK government says that Iran was very likely behind a scare at an air force base in Gloucestershire. The base is called RAF Fairford. A minister called the Home Secretary told MPs about it on 12 October.
On 27 September, police arrested five men near the base. They thought the men might have been planning something dangerous. Two more men were arrested in London. All seven are now free for now, but they must follow rules while the police keep checking. This is called bail.
The government says a powerful Iranian group, the Revolutionary Guard, almost certainly gave the orders. The government has also punished two people with sanctions. These are rules that stop people using money or travelling. Iran says it did nothing wrong.
levels.why: It shows why countries work hard to keep their bases safe.

levels.headline: The UK says Iran was behind a danger at an air base, and Iran says it was not
levels.body:
The UK government says that Iran was very likely behind a scare near an air force base in Gloucestershire called RAF Fairford. On 12 October, a minister called the Home Secretary told MPs that a powerful Iranian group, the Revolutionary Guard, almost certainly gave the orders.

The UK has called in Iran's ambassador and put sanctions on two people, which means stopping them using money in the UK. Iran says it did nothing wrong.
levels.why: It is about keeping people safe and how countries get on.

levels.headline: A scare at an air base
levels.body:
There is an air force base in England called RAF Fairford. In September, police were called because they thought somebody might be planning something dangerous near it. They arrested five men. Later they arrested two more.
On 12 October, a minister told the country that the government thinks Iran was behind it. Iran is a country far away. The minister said a powerful group in Iran, the Revolutionary Guard, almost certainly gave the orders. Iran says that this is not true.
The seven men have not been found guilty of anything. They have been allowed to go home on bail while the police keep checking. The government has also punished two people for helping Iran. It stopped them using money in the UK.
levels.why: Grown-ups work hard to keep everyone safe.

levels.headline: Police look into a worry near an air base
levels.body:
Imagine your school had a worry about safety. Teachers and helpers would check carefully. Something like that happened near an air force base in England called RAF Fairford.
In September, police arrested some men near the base. They thought the men might have been planning to cause harm. Police are still finding out the facts. The men have not been found guilty of anything.
On 12 October, a government minister said the country thinks another country, called Iran, was behind it. Iran says it was not. When countries disagree like this, it can make everyone cross, like when two classes blame each other in the playground. The government has stopped two people from using money in the UK, as a punishment for helping.
levels.why: People work hard to keep us safe, and to find out the truth.

headline: Markets price in a near-certain Bank of England rate rise on 5 November, the first since 2023, with another possible in December

terms.meaning: One hundredth of a percentage point; 25 basis points is a quarter of a point.
The nine Bank of England members who vote on interest rates.
A loan taken out to buy a home.

levels.headline: Markets price in a near-certain Bank of England rate rise on 5 November, the first since 2023, with another possible in December
levels.body:
Financial markets now see a quarter-point rise in the Bank of England's Bank Rate, from 3.75% to 4%, at its meeting on 5 November as close to certain. It would be the first rise since 2023. Traders also price in a further quarter-point rise at the Bank's final meeting of the year in December.
The shift follows UK inflation of 3.5% in September, above forecasts and well over the 2% target. In September the Bank held rates in a 6-3 vote, with three members voting for a 25 basis point rise. Core inflation rose to 2.8% and services inflation was 3.7%.
The Bank is weighing the energy price shock linked to the US-Iran conflict against the risk that higher costs spread into wages and prices. The Federal Reserve raised rates in September and the European Central Bank raised its deposit rate to 2.5%.
The Budget follows on 28 October, with public sector net debt above £3 trillion.
levels.why: Interest rates set the cost of mortgages, loans and savings returns.

levels.headline: A Bank of England rate rise on 5 November looks almost certain, traders say
levels.body:
Traders now treat a quarter-point increase in the Bank of England's interest rate, from 3.75% to 4%, as almost certain at the 5 November meeting. It would be the first rise since 2023. A further quarter-point rise is priced in for the Bank's last meeting of the year, in December.
The change in expectations came after inflation in September hit 3.5%, above forecasts and far over the 2% target. In September the Bank held rates by six votes to three, with the three dissenters wanting a rise. Core inflation went up to 2.8% and services inflation stood at 3.7%.
The Bank must balance an energy price shock, linked to the US-Iran conflict, against the danger of higher costs spreading. The US Federal Reserve raised rates in September and the European Central Bank has raised its deposit rate to 2.5%.
The Budget is due on 28 October.
levels.why: Rate changes feed through to mortgage bills and the cost of loans.

levels.headline: Interest rates look set to rise on 5 November after higher inflation
levels.body:
Investors now think the Bank of England will raise its main interest rate by a quarter of a point, from 3.75% to 4%, on 5 November. That would be its first increase since 2023. They also expect another quarter-point rise in December.
Investors changed their minds after new figures showed inflation at 3.5% in September, above forecasts and well above the Bank's 2% target. When the Bank last met, in September, it kept rates unchanged by six votes to three. The three who lost wanted a rise. Core inflation, which leaves out energy and food, rose to 2.8%.
The Bank has a hard choice. Energy costs have jumped because of the US-Iran conflict. If these costs spread into wages and other prices, inflation could last longer. Central banks in the US and the euro area have also raised rates this year.
levels.why: It may make borrowing dearer and savings pay a little more.

levels.headline: Investors expect the Bank of England to raise interest rates on 5 November
levels.body:
Investors now think the Bank of England will raise its interest rate from 3.75% to 4% at its meeting on 5 November. It would be the first rise since 2023, and traders also expect another in December.
The reason is inflation, which was 3.5% in September, well above the Bank's 2% target. The Bank held rates in September, but three of its nine voting members wanted a rise. Underlying inflation, which leaves out energy and food, has also gone up, to 2.8%.
The Bank has to weigh a jump in energy costs, linked to the conflict involving the United States and Iran, against the risk that it spreads into wages and other prices. The US and the euro area have already raised their rates.
levels.why: A rate rise can make mortgages and loans cost more.

levels.headline: The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates next month
levels.body:
Investors now expect the Bank of England to raise its interest rate on 5 November. The rate would go up by a quarter of a point, from 3.75% to 4%. If it happens, it will be the first rise since 2023. They also expect another rise in December.
The reason is inflation, which is how fast prices rise. In September it was 3.5%. The Bank wants it to be 2%. At the last meeting, in September, the Bank decided to keep rates the same. But three of the nine people voting wanted them to go up.
It is a hard choice. Energy costs have risen because of the conflict involving the United States and Iran. The Bank worries that these higher costs could spread into wages and other prices. The US and the euro area have already put their rates up.
levels.why: Changes in interest rates affect mortgages, loans and savings.

levels.headline: Interest rates in the UK look likely to go up soon
levels.body:
The Bank of England sets the main interest rate for the UK. It is 3.75% now. Many investors think the Bank will raise it to 4% on 5 November. That would be the first rise since 2023. They also think it might go up again in December.
The Bank does this to slow down prices. Prices are rising by 3.5% a year, which is more than the Bank's goal of 2%. When interest rates go up, borrowing costs more, so people and firms often spend less. That can calm prices down.
In September the Bank kept the rate the same. Three of the nine people who vote on this wanted a rise. The cost of energy has gone up because of fighting in the Middle East, and the Bank wants to stop that spreading to other prices.
levels.why: Mortgage and loan payments could go up.

levels.headline: The Bank of England may make borrowing cost more
levels.body:
The Bank of England is a special bank for the whole country. One of its jobs is to stop prices rising too fast. To do this it uses a number called the interest rate. It is 3.75% now. When someone borrows money, they pay back a bit extra. The interest rate helps to decide how much extra.
Many experts think the Bank will raise the rate to 4% on 5 November. Prices are going up by 3.5% a year, but the Bank wants only 2%. Higher interest rates make borrowing cost more. Then people tend to spend less, and prices can calm down.
It might also happen again in December. Nine people vote on the decision. In September, three of them wanted a rise already.
levels.why: It can change what families pay for loans and homes.

levels.headline: Why interest rates in the UK may go up soon
levels.body:
Interest rates are the price of borrowing money. The Bank of England sets the main one, and it is 3.75% now. Many investors think the Bank will raise it to 4% on 5 November. If that happens, it will be the first rise since 2023.
The Bank wants prices to rise by only 2% a year. At the moment they are rising by 3.5%. Making borrowing dearer encourages people to spend less, which can slow prices down.
The Bank also looks at energy, which has become dearer because of fighting in the Middle East. It wants to stop that spreading to other prices. Nine people vote, and in September three already wanted a rise.
levels.why: It changes what families pay on loans and mortgages.

levels.headline: Why borrowing money may cost more soon
levels.body:
When grown-ups borrow money, they pay a bit extra to say thank you. The extra is called interest. A special bank, the Bank of England, decides on a number that guides how much interest people pay. The number is 3.75% now.
Prices in Britain are rising quite fast. Things cost 3.5% more than last year. The Bank would like that to be only 2%. If borrowing costs more, people usually spend less, and prices can slow down. So many experts think the Bank will raise the number to 4% on 5 November.
This would be the first rise in a few years. Nine people vote on it. In September, three of them already wanted a rise, but most did not.
levels.why: It affects how much grown-ups pay back on loans.

levels.headline: Why the bank might change a number
levels.body:
Imagine you lend a friend a toy. You might ask for a little extra back, like a sweet, to say thank you. Borrowing money works like that. The extra is called interest.
There is a big bank for the whole country, called the Bank of England. It picks a number that guides how much extra people pay when they borrow. Right now the number is 3.75. Many grown-ups think the bank will pick a bigger number on 5 November, which is 4.
Why would it do that? Because prices are going up faster than the bank would like. If borrowing costs more, people spend a bit less, and prices calm down, like turning down a loud radio.
levels.why: It decides how much grown-ups pay when they borrow.

headline: Brent crude settles at $108.82 as Iran war and Gulf attacks keep oil above $100

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for oil.
A narrow sea passage in the Gulf through which much of the world's oil is shipped.
Oil stored by governments to release during a supply shortage.

levels.headline: Brent crude settles at $108.82 as Iran war and Gulf attacks keep oil above $100
levels.body:
Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, added 3 cents to settle at $108.82 a barrel on 21 October, after settling at $108.79 on 20 October when it touched a five-month high of $111.99. Trading Economics put it at about $111 on 22 October, roughly 70% higher than a year ago.
The main driver is the war involving Iran. Iran has escalated attacks on tankers in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman, and Houthi militants have claimed strikes on Saudi airports and Aramco facilities.
There are some offsets. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Gulf crude flows have recovered to about 80% of pre-war levels, and G7 countries agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude from emergency reserves.
Sources differ slightly on exact levels because they report different times and contracts. The high oil price feeds directly into fuel and inflation figures, including the UK's 3.5% rate.
levels.why: Oil prices feed into petrol, heating and inflation worldwide.

levels.headline: Oil stays above $108 a barrel as attacks on Gulf shipping continue
levels.body:
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, closed at $108.82 a barrel on 21 October, up 3 cents. A day earlier it settled at $108.79 after reaching a five-month high of $111.99. By 22 October Trading Economics showed it near $111, around 70% above a year ago.
The price is being driven by the war involving Iran. Iran has stepped up attacks on tankers in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman, and Houthi militants say they attacked Saudi airports and Aramco sites.
Some factors ease the pressure. The US Energy Secretary said crude flows from the Gulf are back to about 80% of their pre-war level, and G7 countries agreed to release 100 million barrels from emergency reserves.
Figures vary between sources because of timing and contracts. Dear oil is pushing up fuel costs and inflation in countries such as the UK.
levels.why: Dearer oil raises fuel bills and keeps inflation high.

levels.headline: Oil price stays high at about $109 a barrel because of the war involving Iran
levels.body:
The price of Brent crude, the main international oil benchmark, ended 21 October at $108.82 a barrel. The day before it had touched $111.99, the highest in five months. By 22 October it was near $111, about 70% more than a year ago.
The cause is the war involving Iran. Iran has attacked more tankers in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman, and Houthi militants say they hit Saudi airports and Aramco sites.
Some things are helping. The US Energy Secretary says oil flowing out of the Gulf has recovered to around 80% of what it was before the war. G7 countries have also agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from emergency stores.
Different sources give slightly different numbers.
levels.why: It pushes up petrol prices and the cost of goods.

levels.headline: Oil stays at about $109 a barrel as the war involving Iran goes on
levels.body:
Brent crude, the main world price for oil, ended 21 October at $108.82 a barrel. The day before, it touched a five-month high of $111.99. It is about 70% dearer than a year ago.
The reason is the war involving Iran. Iran has attacked tankers in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman. Houthi fighters say they hit Saudi airports and oil sites. The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow sea route that many oil ships use.
The US Energy Secretary says oil leaving the Gulf is back to about 80% of its pre-war level, and G7 countries agreed to release 100 million barrels from emergency stores. Sources give slightly different prices.
levels.why: Oil prices decide how much petrol and many goods cost.

levels.headline: Oil costs about $109 a barrel as fighting in the Gulf continues
levels.body:
A barrel of Brent crude oil, the main world price, cost $108.82 at the end of trading on 21 October. The day before, it reached $111.99, which was the highest for five months. It is about 70% dearer than a year ago.
Oil is dear because of the war involving Iran. Iran has attacked more oil tankers in the waters of the Gulf, and the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route used by many ships. Houthi fighters say they have attacked Saudi airports and oil sites.
There is some good news. The US says the amount of oil leaving the Gulf is back to about 80% of what it was before the war. And rich countries in the G7 agreed to let out 100 million barrels from their emergency oil stores.
The sources give slightly different prices.
levels.why: Expensive oil means dearer petrol, flights and heating.

levels.headline: Oil is very expensive right now because of fighting in the Middle East
levels.body:
Oil is the thick, dark liquid that gets turned into petrol and diesel. It is sold by the barrel. This week one barrel of the main kind, called Brent, cost about $109. A year ago it cost much less. It is about 70% dearer.
The reason is a war involving Iran. Iran has attacked oil ships in the waters near the Gulf. Another group, the Houthis, say they have attacked places in Saudi Arabia. Many ships carry oil through a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz, so any danger there pushes up the price.
Some things are helping. The US says oil leaving the Gulf is back to about four fifths of what it was. And some rich countries said they will let out 100 million barrels from their emergency stores.
levels.why: It makes petrol and many other things cost more.

levels.headline: Oil costs a lot because of a war
levels.body:
Oil is a liquid that we use to make petrol and diesel for cars and lorries. It is sold in big barrels. This week a barrel cost about $109. That is much more than a year ago.
The reason is a war in the Middle East that involves Iran. Boats that carry oil have been attacked. Some of them travel through a narrow stretch of sea called the Strait of Hormuz. When it is dangerous, fewer boats go, and oil gets scarce. When something gets scarce, it costs more.
Some countries are trying to help. The United States says more oil is flowing again, about four fifths of how much there was before. And some countries said they will let out 100 million barrels that they keep stored for emergencies.
levels.why: Dear oil makes many things in the shops cost more.

levels.headline: Oil is dear because of a war near the Gulf
levels.body:
Oil is what we turn into petrol and diesel. It is sold by the barrel, and this week a barrel of the main kind, called Brent, cost about $109. That is around 70% more than a year ago.
There is a war involving Iran. Ships carrying oil have been attacked in the Gulf. Many ships must pass through a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. When it feels unsafe, fewer ships go, so there is less oil to buy and the price goes up.
Some countries are helping. They have agreed to let out 100 million barrels from their emergency stores, and the US says more oil is flowing again.
levels.why: Dear oil can make petrol and shop prices go up.

levels.headline: Oil is dear because of fighting far away
levels.body:
Oil is a thick liquid from under the ground. Cars, lorries and planes use it to make fuel. This week oil costs a lot of money, much more than last year.
There is a war in a faraway part of the world, near a country called Iran. Boats that carry oil have been attacked. Many boats must go through a narrow bit of sea called the Strait of Hormuz. If it is not safe, fewer boats go. Then there is less oil to buy, so people pay more for it.
Some rich countries have helped. They keep oil stored away for emergencies. They said they would let some of it out, a very big amount. The United States also says more oil is flowing than before.
levels.why: It is why petrol can cost more at the garage.

levels.headline: Why petrol may cost more
levels.body:
Imagine a very big sweet shop with only a few sweets left. Everyone wants one, so the shop asks for more money. Oil is a bit like that right now. Oil is what we turn into petrol for cars.
There is a war far away, near a country called Iran. Boats carrying oil have been attacked, and many boats have to go through a narrow stretch of sea. When it feels unsafe, fewer boats go. So there is less oil for everyone, and it costs more. This week one barrel cost about $109, much more than last year.
Some countries said they would share oil from their emergency stores. That is like the teacher opening the cupboard with spare supplies.
levels.why: It helps explain why things cost more at the shops.

headline: Zelenskyy backs freezing the front line as Kremlin says it is open to new talks after Witkoff meets Putin

terms.meaning: An agreement to stop fighting, at least for a time.
The line where the two armies face each other.
Promises from other countries to help defend Ukraine if attacked again.

levels.headline: Zelenskyy backs freezing the front line as Kremlin says it is open to new talks after Witkoff meets Putin
levels.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that halting fighting along the current front line is the most realistic first step towards ending the war with Russia, opening the way to ceasefire talks. He insisted Kyiv must have a seat at any negotiations and that a deal needs security guarantees from partners including the United States and European allies.
US envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in Saint Petersburg on 21 October. He called the talks constructive and said technical-level discussions among the United States, Russia and Ukraine would continue. The Kremlin said it was open to new three-way talks, though it said recent Ukrainian and European proposals lacked substance. An American detained in Russia, Stephen Hubbard, was freed during the visit.
Obstacles remain. Putin reportedly proposed a summit with Trump and Xi but refuses talks with Zelenskyy, wanting direct talks held in Moscow, which Kyiv rejects. Kyiv and Europe are also angry about a US diesel deal easing sanctions on Russia.
levels.why: The outcome decides security in Europe and affects energy prices and aid.

levels.headline: Zelenskyy backs a front-line freeze as Russia signals openness to new talks
levels.body:
President Zelenskyy has said that stopping the fighting along the present front line is the most realistic way to end the war, and could open the way to ceasefire negotiations. He said Ukraine must be involved in any talks and that a deal needs security guarantees from partners, including the US and European allies.
US envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in Saint Petersburg on 21 October and described the talks as constructive. He said US, Russian and Ukrainian officials would keep talking at a technical level. The Kremlin said it was willing to return to three-way talks but that Ukrainian and European proposals had little substance. Russia also freed an American, Stephen Hubbard.
Differences remain. Putin reportedly wants a summit with Trump and Xi but will not talk to Zelenskyy, and wants direct talks in Moscow, which Kyiv rejects. Kyiv and Europe are angry that the US has eased some sanctions on Russian diesel.
levels.why: Any ceasefire would shape European security and the future of sanctions.

levels.headline: Ukraine's leader backs freezing the front line, and Russia says it is open to talks
levels.body:
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says the most realistic first step to end the war is to stop fighting where the armies are now. This would open the way to talks on a ceasefire. He says Ukraine must have a seat at the table, and any deal needs security guarantees from allies such as the US and European countries.
On 21 October the US envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Saint Petersburg. Witkoff called the talks constructive. The Kremlin said it is open to new three-way talks with the US and Ukraine, but said recent Ukrainian and European ideas lacked substance. An American held in Russia, Stephen Hubbard, was freed.
Big differences remain. Putin refuses to meet Zelenskyy and wants talks in Moscow, which Kyiv rejects. Europe and Ukraine are also unhappy about a US decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel.
levels.why: The war affects security, prices and aid across Europe.

levels.headline: Zelenskyy wants fighting frozen at the front line, and Russia says it is open to talks
levels.body:
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says stopping the fighting along the current front line is the most realistic first step to end the war. After that, ceasefire talks could begin. He wants Ukraine to be at the table and wants security guarantees from allies, including the United States and European countries.
On 21 October, US envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in Saint Petersburg and called the talks constructive. Russia said it would return to three-way talks with the US and Ukraine, and freed an American, Stephen Hubbard.
But Putin refuses to meet Zelenskyy and wants talks in Moscow, which Kyiv rejects. Kyiv and Europe are also unhappy about a US decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel.
levels.why: Peace in Ukraine would make Europe safer and affect energy prices.

levels.headline: Ukraine wants to stop the fighting where it is now, and Russia says it will talk
levels.body:
Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says the best first step to end the war is to stop fighting along the line where the armies are now. This is called freezing the front line. After that, countries could talk about a ceasefire, which is an agreement to stop fighting. He says Ukraine must be at the table and wants promises from allies, including the US, to help keep it safe.
On 21 October, a US envoy called Steve Witkoff met Russia's leader, Vladimir Putin. Witkoff said the meeting went well. Russia says it would take part in new talks with the US and Ukraine. Russia also freed an American teacher, Stephen Hubbard.
But the sides still disagree. Putin will not meet Zelenskyy, and wants the talks in Moscow. Ukraine says no to that.
levels.why: Peace in Ukraine would make Europe safer.

levels.headline: Ukraine and Russia are still far apart, but talks may start again
levels.body:
The war between Russia and Ukraine is still going on. This week, Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said the best first step is to stop the fighting where the armies are now. Then they could talk about a longer peace. He wants Ukraine to be at the table. He also wants other countries to promise to help protect Ukraine in future.
On 21 October, an American helper called Steve Witkoff met Russia's president, Vladimir Putin. Witkoff said it was a good meeting. Russia said it was ready for new talks with the US and Ukraine. An American man who had been held in Russia was let go.
But there are problems. Putin does not want to meet Zelenskyy. He wants talks in Moscow, and Ukraine will not agree to that.
levels.why: It decides if a long, sad war might end.

levels.headline: Leaders talk about stopping the war in Ukraine
levels.body:
There is a war between Russia and Ukraine. Many people have been hurt. This week, the leader of Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said a good first step would be for both sides to stop fighting where they are now. After that, they could talk about peace. He wants his country to be at the talks. He also wants friends, like the United States and countries in Europe, to promise to help keep Ukraine safe.
On 21 October a man from America, Steve Witkoff, met the leader of Russia, Vladimir Putin. Russia says it would like to talk more. It also let an American man go free.
But the leaders still disagree. Putin does not want to meet Zelenskyy, so it is a hard problem.
levels.why: Peace would help families in Ukraine and across Europe.

levels.headline: People try to end the war between Russia and Ukraine
levels.body:
There has been a war between Russia and Ukraine for a long time. This week, Ukraine's president said the best first step is for both sides to stop fighting where they are now. Then they could talk about a longer peace. He wants Ukraine to take part, and wants friends like the United States to promise to help protect it.
An American helper, Steve Witkoff, met Russia's president on 21 October and said the meeting went well. Russia says it will talk more. It also let one American man go free.
But the leaders still disagree about where to talk, and Russia's president will not meet Ukraine's.
levels.why: Ending the war would help families in Ukraine and across Europe.

levels.headline: People are trying to stop a war
levels.body:
A war has been going on between two countries, Russia and Ukraine. Grown-ups want it to stop. This week, the leader of Ukraine said a good first step would be for both sides to stop fighting where they are now. Then they could talk about a longer peace.
Another leader from America sent a helper to meet the leader of Russia. The helper said it went well. Russia said it would talk more. It also let one American go free.
But it is hard. The leaders do not agree about where to meet. The leader of Russia does not want to meet the leader of Ukraine. It is a bit like two children who have had a big argument and do not want to say sorry.
levels.why: Everyone hopes the fighting will stop.

levels.headline: Grown-ups try to end a long argument
levels.body:
Imagine two classes in a big, sad argument that has gone on for a long time. Grown-ups want to help them stop. This is a bit like the war between Russia and Ukraine. Many people have been hurt.
This week, the leader of Ukraine said the first thing to do is for everyone to stop where they are. Then they can talk. A helper from America visited the leader of Russia, and said the talk went well. Russia said it would talk some more.
But the two leaders still do not agree about how to talk. One of them does not want to meet the other. So the grown-ups are still working hard to find a way to be kind and stop the fighting.
levels.why: Everyone hopes the people involved will be safe.

headline: French unions call for 5 November action after talks with PM Lecornu, days after riots and looting

terms.meaning: An organisation that represents workers and negotiates for them.
Jobs paid for by the government, such as teaching.
The interest a government pays to borrow; they rise when investors worry.

levels.headline: French unions call for 5 November action after talks with PM Lecornu, days after riots and looting
levels.body:
Union leaders who met Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday 21 October left the roughly two-and-a-half-hour meeting disappointed and called a large mobilisation for 5 November. CGT leader Sophie Binet said strike action must take over from that date.
The call follows protests on 17 October that turned into riots and looting in several cities, including Paris, Lyon and Marseille. Retail federation head Alexandre Bompard said about 1,500 shops were hit, with a bill of hundreds of millions of euros. French government bond yields rose and the euro weakened as the unrest added to investor worries about France's debt.
The government's 2027 budget targets a fiscal adjustment of 54 billion euros, with part of the savings coming from freezing public sector pay, including for teachers. Earlier student-led protests had been under way in the weeks before.
levels.why: It tests France's government and affects confidence in its finances and the euro.

levels.headline: French unions plan 5 November mobilisation after disappointing talks with the prime minister
levels.body:
Union leaders met Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on 21 October. The meeting lasted about two and a half hours, and they left disappointed. They have called for a large mobilisation on 5 November, and CGT leader Sophie Binet said strikes must take over from that date.
This follows protests on 17 October that turned into riots and looting in several cities. The head of the retail federation, Alexandre Bompard, said about 1,500 shops were hit at a cost of hundreds of millions of euros. headline: Fed and ECB decide on rates next week, with a hold expected but hike risk rising after hot US inflation

terms.meaning: The central bank of the United States.

levels.headline: Fed and ECB decide on rates next week, with a hold expected but hike risk rising after hot US inflation
levels.body:
The US Federal Reserve decides on interest rates on 28 October and the European Central Bank on 29 October. Both are expected to hold rates, although the Fed carries more risk of a rise.
The Fed raised its target range to 3.75% to 4% in September, its first increase since 2023, in a 12-0 vote. Chair Kevin Warsh said inflation has been too high for too long. Futures markets put the chance of an October rise at 15% on 16 October, but a hot US inflation reading since then has roughly doubled traders' bets. Warsh said he was not signalling a decision. US consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year to September, according to one report.
The ECB raised its deposit rate to 2.5% on 10 September. Eurozone inflation has climbed to 3.8%, a three-year high. Traders expect a hold on 29 October and a rise in December. The euro has slid to its weakest against the dollar since mid-May 2025.
levels.why: These decisions shape borrowing costs and currency moves around the world.

levels.headline: Central banks in the US and Europe face rate decisions next week as inflation stays high
levels.body:
The US Federal Reserve will announce its interest rate decision on 28 October, and the European Central Bank on 29 October. Most traders expect both to hold rates, but the risk of a Fed rise has grown.
The Fed lifted its target range to 3.75% to 4% in September, the first rise since 2023, by a vote of 12-0. Chair Kevin Warsh said inflation had been too high for too long. levels.why: Central bank choices affect mortgages, loans and exchange rates worldwide.

levels.headline: US and European central banks meet next week, with inflation worries growing
levels.body:
The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, makes its next decision on 28 October. The European Central Bank follows on 29 October. Most traders think both will leave interest rates alone, but the chance of a US rise has gone up.

The ECB raised its deposit rate to 2.5% in September. Inflation in the countries that use the euro is 3.8%, the highest in three years. Traders expect another rise in December. The euro has fallen against the dollar.
levels.why: Interest rate decisions affect loans, savings and the value of currencies.

levels.headline: US and European central banks meet next week, with a hold expected but a US hike possible

levels.why: These decisions set borrowing costs and affect currencies.

levels.headline: Big central banks decide on interest rates next week
levels.body:
Two big central banks will decide on interest rates next week. The US Federal Reserve will announce on 28 October. The European Central Bank, which looks after the euro, will announce on 29 October. Most investors expect both to leave rates as they are, but the Fed might raise its rate.
The Fed raised its rate to between 3.75% and 4% in September, for the first time since 2023. Its leader, Kevin Warsh, said prices had been rising too fast for too long. Since then, new figures showed that US prices are still rising quickly, at 3.7% a year, according to one report. So more people now think the Fed could raise rates again.
In Europe, prices are rising by 3.8% a year. The ECB raised its rate in September, to 2.5%. Investors expect it to wait until December.
levels.why: These choices change what people pay to borrow, in many countries.

levels.headline: Two big banks will decide about interest rates next week
levels.body:
Central banks are special banks that look after a country's money. Two big ones will make choices next week. One is in the United States and is called the Federal Reserve. It decides on 28 October. The other, the European Central Bank, decides on 29 October.
Both can change an interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. Raising it makes borrowing cost more, which can slow down rising prices. Prices have been rising fast in both places. In the US, they are up 3.7% in a year. In the countries that use the euro, they are up 3.8%.
Most people think both banks will leave the rate as it is this time. But the American bank might raise it. Both have already raised rates this autumn.
levels.why: It changes how much people pay to borrow money.

levels.headline: Banks in America and Europe will think about interest rates
levels.body:
Some banks look after a whole country's money. They are called central banks. Next week two of them will meet. One is in America, the Federal Reserve. It will decide on 28 October. The other looks after the euro and is in Europe. It decides on 29 October.
They each have a special number called the interest rate. It is the price for borrowing money. Prices in both places have gone up a lot in a year, so the banks have already put their rates up once. Most experts think they will keep them the same this time. But the American one might go up.
When the number is higher, borrowing money costs more. Then people spend less, and prices can slow down.
levels.why: The rates change how much families pay for loans.

levels.headline: Two big banks may change the price of borrowing money

Most experts think both will keep the rate the same this time. The American bank might raise it, though. We will know soon.
levels.why: It changes what families pay on loans.

levels.headline: Two big banks will pick a number next week
levels.body:

One bank is in America. The other is in Europe. Prices there have gone up quite a lot in a year, so both banks have already made their number bigger once. A bigger number makes borrowing cost more. Then people tend to spend less, and prices may slow down.
Most experts think both banks will keep the number the same next week. But the American bank might make it bigger. We will find out on 28 and 29 October.
levels.why: It decides how much grown-ups pay on loans.

levels.headline: Banks choose a number
levels.body:

Next week, two big banks will choose their numbers. One is in America. One is in Europe. If the number is bigger, borrowing costs more. Then people spend less, and prices stop rising so fast.
Prices have been rising in both places, so both banks put the number up already. Most grown-ups think they will keep it the same this time. But the American bank might put it up again. It will tell everybody on 28 October.
levels.why: The number changes what families pay for borrowing.

headline: Nigeria confirms first Ebola case as African health ministers prepare crisis talks

levels.headline: Nigeria confirms first Ebola case as African health ministers prepare crisis talks
levels.body:
Nigeria confirmed its first case of Ebola on Tuesday 20 October, making it the fourth country to report a case in the current outbreak. The patient is linked to a traveller from Uganda who entered Nigeria on 5 October and was first treated for malaria but failed to recover, which raised suspicion among doctors.
Authorities are tracing 44 contacts, mostly healthcare workers, along with the patient's spouse, a Swiss national. Uganda, which declared itself Ebola-free in July after recording 20 cases, denies the case originated there. It says travelling through Uganda does not show infection took place there, and where the exposure happened is under investigation.
The Africa CDC has called for urgent action and is convening African health ministers to coordinate the response. Its director general, Jean Kaseya, said the response must move faster, with stronger coordination, greater solidarity and decisive political leadership.
This account relies on a single outlet, so check later updates.
levels.why: Early detection and coordination are vital to stop Ebola spreading.

headline: China's economy grows 4.5% in July to September on strong exports, while domestic demand stays weak

levels.headline: China's economy grows 4.5% in July to September on strong exports, while domestic demand stays weak
levels.body:
China's economy grew 4.5% in the third quarter, from July to September, according to Euronews, with strong exports carrying the figure while domestic weakness persists.
After a 36% jump in exports last month, China has a trade surplus of $938 billion for January to September. It is on course to top last year's record surplus of $1.2 trillion. Higher US tariffs have dented bilateral trade, pushing Chinese exporters toward Southeast Asia, Latin America and Europe. The EU is pressing Beijing over trade imbalances, and EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič is expected to travel to Beijing next month.
In late September the US and China extended their trade truce to 10 January, shorter than many analysts expected, and both sides named about $30 billion of goods each for possible tariff cuts. One analysis called the outcomes quite limited and tentative. A possible Trump-Xi meeting could take place alongside the APEC meeting in Shenzhen in November.

Exports rose by 36% last month. Over the first nine months of the year, China sold $938 billion more than it bought, a trade surplus. It is likely to beat last year's record of $1.2 trillion. levels.headline: China's economy grew by 4.5%, helped by selling goods abroad
